These and other compromises and incompatibilities at the interface of the two systems may be addressed by an intermediary providing ChaaS. This provider can be visualized as a conduit between the supply side (electricity provider) and the demand side (charging customer), facilitating flows of information, electric power, and capital between the two sides. Such a framework allows ChaaS to provide a range of functions. A simple example might be for a ChaaS provider to pay for the purchase and installation costs for residential EVSE and assess a usage fee, thereby easing customers’ capital expenditure burdens. A more complex example might be to install and dispatch distributed energy resources (DERs) for supplemental power, manage vehicle charging and discharging, and provide and sell ancillary services to the electric grid, thereby easing utilities’ load integration challenges. ChaaS seeks to provide value to electricity suppliers and EV customers by reducing inefficiencies at the electricity/transportation system interface and/or assuming risks that would otherwise be incumbent on the electricity supplier or EV customer. Risks transferable from the EV customer to the ChaaS operator may include those of unexpected electricity costs, equipment upkeep costs, and obsolescence costs [26, 23, 22, 34, 34, 30, 25, 33]. Risks transferable from the electricity provider and/or site owner to the ChaaS operator can include those of low equipment utilization and variability in power demand [30, 31, 25, 29, 24, 33]. In addition to providing efficiency improvement and risk transfer, ChaaS can help to balance the costs and benefits of transportation electrification. This might be thought of as correcting a potential market failure, and as such is not part of the ordinary business case of ChaaS but instead might be of interest to policymakers and regulators. Functions of charging-as-a-service In the general business case for ChaaS, a ChaaS provider assesses fees to its customers- in exchange for the use of EVSE, and for related services, such as equipment installation, integration, upkeep, monitoring, and management.
